title: Burnout & Depression: Development of an early warning system and AI advisor for healthcare workers to assess and manage stress, monitor longterm trajectories, and predict outcomes using multivariate and AI-based extraction of specific biomarkers and mHealth technologies.
summary:
The StressPredict4Nurses study investigates the relationships between physiological stress parameters (e.g., heart rate variability, sleep quality) and psychosocial stressors in nursing staff. The aim is to develop and validate an AI-supported digital early warning system that can detect work-related stress at an early stage and thereby contribute to the prevention of depression or burnout.

Stress indicators of nursing staff at the University Hospital Jena are recorded over a period of six months using wearables (Polar H10, Polar Verity Sense) as well as a companion app (Preventicus Nightwatch). In addition, standardized psychometric questionnaires and qualitative interviews will be conducted (including BDI-II, PSS-10, BFI-10, SCL-90, BSW5, ISAK, BAT, and SCQ). This study is a collaboration between Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Preventicus GmbH, Significo GmbH, and Jena University Hospital.

interventions.name: Nursing staff at Jena University Hospital, organized into two observational cohorts – pilot cohort (n = 60) and validation cohort (n = 60). The study will be conducted at Jena University Hospital. This is a collaborative study with Significo GmbH, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Preventicus Gm

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•    Healthy nursing staff between the ages of 18 and 65 with no known chronic illnesses.
•    No acute illnesses or infections at the time of the study.
•    No medications that could influence physiological parameters.
•    Willingness to participate in the study and ability to give consent.
•    Regular nursing duties to reflect typical working conditions.
Exclusion criteria:
•    Presence of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or other chronic conditions.
•    Pregnancy or breastfeeding.
•    Acute infections or fever.
•    Use of medications that affect heart rate, blood pressure, or other physiological parameters.
•    Physical limitations that could interfere with the measurements (e.g., skin injuries at measurement sites).
